title: How do you track actual job costs against your estimate?
summary: To track actual job costs against your estimate, turn the approved estimate into a budget, tie every receipt, crew hour, and change order to the line it belongs to, and compare the two every week while the job's still running.
body_markdown:
It's 6:40 on a Friday and you're sitting in the truck with a stack of receipts from the supply house. The bathroom job felt tight all week. You just don't know if it's tight by $400 or by $4,000. That gap between a feeling and a number is where margin goes. Here's how to close it, from the approved estimate to the final invoice.


## Why do actual costs end up different from the estimate?


Actual costs drift from the estimate because prices move. So small items go unpriced and the scope changes. Then labor runs longer than planned.


- **Material prices move:** An estimate written in August can be stale by October.[Construction Dive reported](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/cost-spikes-construction-materials-producer-price-index/830165/) in September 2026 that copper wire is up 27.2% year over year, and the Associated Builders and Contractors chief economist said ongoing input price increases are "likely to weigh on profitability over the next several months."
- **The small stuff:** Caulk, brackets, fasteners, and tape rarely make it into a hand estimate, and they always make it onto the receipt.
- **Scope changes:** One more outlet, a wider doorway, a different tile. Each one is small until you add them up.
- **Labor:** The demo that looked like a day and ran two.


> The average net profit margin for remodelers in 2024 is 6.3%, according to[NAHB's latest study](https://eyeonhousing.org/2026/04/remodelers-saw-profit-margin-gains-in-2024/) . Gross margin averaged 29.9%.


On a $40,000 job, a 6.3% net margin is about $2,500 of profit. A few unlogged supply runs can take a big bite out of that. But tracking costs as they happen keeps you in control of the margin you priced in.


## How do you turn an estimate into a job budget?


Use the approved estimate as the baseline, with the same sections, the same lines, and the same totals, so every cost you log later maps to something you already priced.


- **Keep the lines you priced:** Don't build a second list. Budget by section and by line item so a surprise shows up in the exact spot it happened.
- **Add change orders as they're signed:** The budget should move with the contract, so you're always comparing against the current price.
- **Pick a check-in day:** One day a week, same time. Friday afternoon works well, since the week's receipts are all in the truck.

Track materials, crew hours, change orders, and daily site notes, and tie each one to an estimate line the day it happens.


> "The biggest killer in construction for margin is the big-box runs."
> [Tony DiSilvestro, Ynot Build](https://handoff.ai/blog/how-a-thirty-year-builder-bids-and-wins-from-the-driveway)

## Should you use a spreadsheet or software for tracking job costs?


### What each one does well


A spreadsheet works for one or two jobs when you've got an evening each week to keep it current. Software starts earning its place once costs arrive from the truck, the supply house, and the crew at the same time.


- **Spreadsheet:** Free, familiar, and fully yours. It runs on you typing in every receipt and rebuilding the layout for each new job.
- **Accounting software:** Your accountant keeps the books, and that's the right home for them. Job costing is the line-by-line view while the job's still running.
- **A contractor job tracking app:** It starts from your estimate, so the budget's built before the first receipt shows up.[Handoff's project management](https://handoff.ai/project-management) covers the schedule, budget, crew hours, change orders, daily logs, and client portal in one app, on Pro and Scale.


Handoff gives you one system from estimate to completion, so the numbers don't live in five places.


## How often should you compare actual costs to your estimate?


Compare weekly while the job's running, any time a big purchase or signed change order lands, and once more when the job closes.


Ten minutes a week is all it takes. Look at what you've spent, what's left, and which lines are over. Say your estimate has $4,200 for tile and setting materials, and the receipts so far total $4,650. That's $450 over with the floor still to finish, so you can adjust the rest of the job. Found at the final invoice, that margin's gone.


Here are two others to stay on top of:


1. **The trigger check:** After a supply house run over an amount you set, and whenever a client signs a change order.
2. **The close-out check:** When the job wraps, compare final costs to the estimate and note which lines moved. Your next estimate starts from real numbers. ## Other FAQs about job costing


**What's the difference between an estimate and job costing?**


An estimate is the price you plan to charge, based on the costs you expect. Job costing is tracking what the job actually costs as it runs. Comparing the two shows your real margin on each job and tells you what to change in the next estimate.


**Can you track job costs from your phone?**


Yes. Handoff has iOS and Android apps, so you can manage a job from the truck, and your crew can clock in from the app (Time Tracking is on Pro and Scale). A contractor job tracking app should work where you work, and that's the job site.


**Do small jobs need job costing?**


Yes, in a lighter form. A $10,000 job has the same supply runs and the same surprises, just fewer lines. Even one check at the end shows you which lines moved.
